item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
They don't contradict each other at all. There is no way for the "form" or "state" to be detected, and it doesn't manifest visually, aurally, or physically, but they can test that it exists quite easily. Have a conversation in a soundproofed room down the hall and ask the subject upon waking what the conversation was about. To verify it can be used to "see" things as well, ask what color tie the researchers were wearing, or write something on a pad of paper and have the subject tell what was on it.

Anyway, those statements aren't contradictory because they're talking about different aspects of the thing/its capabilities. It definitely could be worded better because I had to think for a second after reading it to make sure I understood what was being said.

I actually rather like the concept, but there definitely are tonal issues. I'm going to -1 in the hopes it gets the attention it needs instead of giving a +1 that could potentially contribute to keeping it forever in this state.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
…You've got a point. That second line directly contradicts the first. Perhaps the paragraph could be rephrased something like this?

When SCP-438 is worn as originally designed, the wearer falls into a comatose state combined with a continuous out-of-body experience (OBE); the subject’s mind effectively becomes a disembodied consciousness. No method available to the Foundation can detect the consciousness in this state. However, post-use interviews with SCP-438 subjects indicate that the experience is quite real — the consciousness retains full sensory perception and is capable of traversing vast distances instantly and effortlessly, as proved by subjects' ability to report accurately on distant events that occurred during the SCP-438 coma. Memory is comparable to the subject's unaltered capacity.

That helps clarify the difference between testing to detect the consciousness itself, which doesn't work, and testing whether the subjects actually perceive the world while comatose, which does.

SCP-438 has obvious applications in the field of espionage and scientific exploration, but carries considerable risk, both to the subject and to sensitive data on the part of the agency employing the item. It is fortunate that the subject must trust his or her comrades in order to use the item safely; if there is reason to suspect the subject's loyalty, the item may simply be left on until the subject has expired.

I don't agree with his paragraph existing in the article. I don't like the concept of using SCPs much, so take this how you well.

Overall… could be taken farther, as it is, somewhat boring.
